IT'S BEEN AN unusual time. At the end of October, the New York Times broke a story about Jensen Huang, the founder and CEO of Nvidia. The accusation: that he may have been romantically involved with a woman who was an industrial spy for the Chinese government. After some initial denials, Huang acknowledged the relationship. A few weeks later, the Times reported that Huang may have had a second affair, this one with an Nvidia employee. Huang resigned the next day.
Corporate scandals are nothing new, but this one was unusual in that, before the news broke, Nvidia had been the most valuable company in the world. At its peak, its market capitalization had been $5.8 trillion. And Huang had achieved a sort of celebrity status. Regularly clad in leather jackets, he would happily sign his fans’ clothing and autograph their computers. He was the pied piper of the artificial intelligence boom.
After Huang resigned, Nvidia’s stock went into freefall, declining seven days in a row. Last Friday alone, it dropped 14%. And because of its size and its role at the center of the AI ecosystem, this triggered a broader market selloff.
Even when it reported strong earnings last week—with revenue doubling from last year—the stock continued its downward slide. And when things looked like they couldn’t get any worse, the Securities and Exchange Commission announced that it had opened an investigation, and Treasury secretary Scott Bessent questioned whether the company had been violating export laws: “What was the culture at Nvidia and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?”
Facing criticism from all sides, Nvidia’s board reaffirmed last week that the company had no intention of reinstating Huang. But then, this past Monday morning, the board did just that. Huang was greeted by a cheering crowd as he re-entered company headquarters. By the end of the day, Nvidia’s stock had risen more than 31%. In dollar terms, the company regained $1 trillion in value.
What lessons can investors learn from this story?
First, it helps illustrate a flaw in a theory known as the efficient market hypothesis, which argues that market prices reflect all available information. The reality is that markets have selective attention. For more than a year, there’s been concern about “circular” deals among companies in Nvidia’s orbit. Nvidia has, for example, made large investments in OpenAI, which has enabled OpenAI, in turn, to purchase more chips from Nvidia. There’s nothing necessarily wrong with these relationships, but they’ve led to questions about the sustainability of the AI boom.
For a variety of reasons, though, even when a risk like this is well known, sometimes it just doesn’t register in the stock price. As recently as October, before the Nvidia scandal, The Wall Street Journal carried a story titled “Is the Flurry of Circular AI Deals a Win-Win—or Sign of a Bubble?” In a well-reasoned analysis, the story revisited the risks to the broader market of these circular deals, which it likened to “a plate of spaghetti.” But stories like this did nothing to slow the market’s momentum.
The problem, though, is that investor sentiment can shift suddenly, and usually without warning. In some cases, there’s a trigger, as there was this time. But oftentimes there isn’t. Ask investors what triggered the tech-stock selloff that began in 2000, and they’ll have a hard time identifying a single factor. Like a flock of birds, sometimes investors just decide to change direction all at once.
As the WSJ noted in its October writeup, things can work just fine, “until they don’t.” We see this phenomenon all the time, where risks are seemingly just ignored. Consider, for example, what’s been going on recently in Saudi Arabia. The Houthis, a terrorist group backed by Iran, have been attacking the Saudi capital. Twice in the past week, they’ve hit the tallest building in Riyadh with drones, attempting a September 11 sort of attack.
For now, Riyadh hasn’t responded, but it certainly could. There’s a non-zero chance of an open war between Saudi Arabia and Iran, and yet, that risk just isn’t receiving much focus. Why not? One explanation is what psychologists call rational ignorance. That’s the idea that there’s just too much going on in the world for anyone to truly pay attention to it all. As investors, it’s important to recognize the reality of this phenomenon. The efficient market hypothesis tells us that stock prices reflect all available information, but the reality is that markets have selective attention such that they only sometimes reflect available information.
The events at Nvidia help us appreciate another aspect of market dynamics. You may have seen charts illustrating the impact on investment returns if an investor had missed just a handful of the market’s best days over time. According to an analysis by Fidelity Investments, for example, investors who missed just the five best days between 1988 and 2025 would have seen their portfolio gains reduced by nearly 40%.
These illustrations are common, and I use them myself, but I’ll acknowledge they can seem abstract and maybe even a little hard to believe. But the events of this past week help us see how that phenomenon plays out.
On Monday, when Huang returned to Nvidia, it wasn’t just his company’s stock that rose. The S&P 500 overall gained nearly 5%. To put that in context, the average return of the S&P 500 historically has been 10% per year. This helps us see why it’s so important to avoid responding too quickly to the news of the day, because it's often just that—today's news, only to be replaced by a potentially different narrative tomorrow.
Jack Bogle, founder of the Vanguard Group, used to say that when markets became volatile, investors’ best move was counterintuitive: “Don’t do something; just stand there.” To be sure, he was saying it with a smile, but it’s almost universally the right advice.
